Al-Ghazali. Living from ten fifty-eight to eleven eleven, Al-Ghazali was a Persian Islamic philosopher, theologian, and jurist who became the greatest intellectual authority of the medieval Islamic world. Known as the Proof of Islam, he synthesized Aristotelian logic with Islamic theology, defending orthodox Islamic doctrine against rationalist challenges.

Born in Khorasan, Persia, he trained in Islamic jurisprudence, theology, and philosophy in Baghdad, then became a teacher and advisor to the Abbasid caliph. He became the principal defender of orthodox Islam against the rationalist Mutazilite school, which argued that reason alone could derive Islamic truth without revelation. He authored Incoherence of the Philosophers, a systematic refutation of Aristotelian philosophy as applied to Islamic doctrine. He argued that philosophers could not prove the eternity of the world or deny divine omniscience.

Al-Ghazali stressed the limits of reason in theology. He asserted that matters like the nature of God's attributes and divine predestination must be accepted on faith, not rationalism. He became deeply influenced by Sufism—Islamic mysticism—and integrated contemplative, devotional practice into orthodox Islamic theology. This synthesis elevated Sufism's status within Islam significantly.

He authored The Revival of Islamic Sciences, an encyclopedic synthesis of Islamic law, ethics, and spirituality that became a canonical reference for centuries. He even engaged in intellectual debates with philosophers like Averroes, who represented the continued rationalist tradition in Islamic Spain. Averroes replied to Al-Ghazali's Incoherence with his own work called Incoherence of the Incoherence. His massive philosophical and devotional works profoundly shaped Islamic thought, Sufism, and Islamic law for centuries, establishing him as one of the most influential thinkers in Islamic history.
